tier_reason: First-party Google case study on the proprietary Sheets calculation engine (WasmGC build vs the J2CL JavaScript build in Chrome), seen only through WebSearch snippets; no hardware, flags or public harness, so not reproducible and capped at C. The J2CL repo's benchmarking/ harness (j2 bench on Closure, Wasm and JVM) publishes no results.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Final WasmGC build of the Sheets calculation worker about 2x faster calculation than the JavaScript build, described as a 4x improvement over the first WasmGC build (snippet only); the JavaScript build had been more than 3x slower than the Java build on the server (snippet only). The record's 'speculative inlining plus devirtualization cut Chrome calculation time by about 40%' figure was not visible in the snippets seen by the verifier and is unconfirmed here.
corrections.caveats: Snippet only: web.dev (and its web.developers.google.cn mirror) do not resolve here, so the case study was not opened; the 2x and 4x figures were read from WebSearch snippets of the page, and press coverage (heise, 9to5Google, mezha.ua) only repeats Google's claim. First-party Google claim on the proprietary Sheets calculation engine, not reproducible from the repo; no hardware, Chrome version or flags stated; the gain is reported for desktop Chrome and Edge. The 2x is not attributable to J2CL alone: it combines J2CL's WasmGC backend, Binaryen wasm-opt, V8 engine work (speculative inlining and devirtualization are V8 optimizations) and Sheets code changes; the same case study reports that moving regex from a WasmGC-compiled re2j to Chrome's native RegExp made regex operations nearly 100x faster (record's figure, not re-seen). Since the JavaScript build was more than 3x slower than Java, the 2x gain recovers only part of that gap. The repo README calls Wasm support 'fully working but ... work-in-progress'. The repo has a benchmarking/ folder (benchmarking/README.md: `j2 bench <name>` runs Closure, Wasm and JVM targets, e.g. octane Box2dBenchmark) but no published results were seen.

notes: Real and notable (1.4k stars, production use in Google Sheets), Apache-2.0, last commit 2026-10-11 confirmed. Shortcomings: snippet-only evidence from an unopened first-party page, proprietary workload, no methodology, speed-up shared with V8 and Binaryen work; the 40% sub-claim could not be re-confirmed.

tier_reason: README 'Sample result output' prints Benchmark.js ops/sec for kiwi vs Cassowary.js from the repo's own harness bench/main.js (npm run bench), but gives no hardware, Node.js version, date or browser, so first-party with partial methodology: C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Creation: Cassowary.js 2,597 ops/sec vs kiwi 26,243 ops/sec (printed as about 10.11x faster); the 'kiwi new API' row is 20,840 ops/sec (about 8.0x, derived from page data). Solving: Cassowary.js 260,002 vs kiwi 595,455 ops/sec (printed as about 2.29x faster).
corrections.caveats: The numbers are a 'sample result output' in the README with no hardware, Node.js version or date; they are not in the predecessor IjzerenHein/kiwi.js README, so they were added by the LUME maintainer after May 2021. First-party benchmark with partial methodology. The harness (bench/main.js) builds the same two-subview layout in both libraries and the solving test runs two suggestValue/resolve cycles on each, so the work looks equivalent, but the result checks are commented out. The category fit is weak: the speed-up is a TypeScript implementation over another JS library (Cassowary.js), not WebAssembly; the AssemblyScript/WebAssembly build has only been announced since May 2021. Lineage: the repo continues IjzerenHein/kiwi.js (its git history includes IjzerenHein's commits and the commit 'Removed c++ and python code', and the kiwi.js README now says it is unmaintained and points to lume/kiwi), which was a TypeScript port of nucleic/kiwi's C++ solver. Licence text is in COPYING.txt (Modified BSD, BSD-3-Clause; there is no LICENSE file), matching package.json.

notes: Numbers match the README exactly; the harness compares like for like in Node.js. Shortcomings: no hardware or runtime version, sample output of unknown date, weak fit for the wasm-langs category (no Wasm build exists), stale (last commit 2025-05-20), 214 stars.

tier_reason: The only figure is a preliminary first-party '10-20% faster than js_of_ocaml' from the late-2023 ocaml-wasm forum update, seen via WebSearch snippets (discuss.ocaml.org, lwn.net and ocsigen.org do not resolve here); the repo's benchmarks/ harness exists but no published results with CPU, Node.js version or flags were seen, so C.

corrections.workload: OCaml programs compiled once by wasm_of_ocaml and once by js_of_ocaml and timed in Node.js. The repo's benchmarks/ directory is the harness: `make bench` runs microbenchmarks plus benchmark-fiat-crypto, benchmark-ocamlc, benchmark-partial-render-table, benchmark-camlboy and benchmark-others for current-bench; report-wasm-cb.config charts wasm_of_ocaml times on node and report-jsoo-cb.config charts js_of_ocaml times on node as a separate series (no shared reference line); run.config runs node with --no-liftoff. Which workloads the quoted 10-20% figure covers is not stated.
corrections.caveats: Snippet only: the forum post (discuss.ocaml.org), its LWN repeat and the ocsigen.org performance page do not resolve here, so the 10-20% figure was read from WebSearch snippets; it is a 2023 preliminary result with no published programs or methodology, and later versions (6.x, many 'Runtime/Wasm: faster ...' CHANGES entries) are not quantified. A newer ocaml.org post (April 2026) also could not be opened. The repo harness records timings but states no CPU model, Node.js version or flags (run.config is tuned per machine). Output requires Wasm GC, tail-call and exception-handling support (Chrome 119, Node.js 22, Firefox 122, Safari 18.2 or newer); effect handlers default to JSPI, which the README says is slower for performing effects than --effects=cps. Licence: dune-project declares GPL-2.0-or-later and LGPL-2.1-or-later WITH OCaml-LGPL-linking-exception; the LICENSE file puts the compiler, lib, runtime, toplevel and tools under LGPL 2.1 with a static-linking exception.

notes: Real project (1.1k stars shared with js_of_ocaml, last commit 2026-10-09, binaryen 119+ requirement confirmed in README.md). The record's claim that report-wasm-cb.config uses js_of_ocaml as its reference was wrong and is corrected in workload. Shortcomings: snippet-only, preliminary 2023 figure, no methodology, modest gain.
